blocks.text: Independence is the specific condition under which two events do not influence each other's probabilities at all. This lesson builds directly on conditional probability and the general multiplication rule from probability rules, sharpening both into a single precise test you can apply to any pair of events: are they independent, or does one carry information about the other.

blocks.caption: The core distinction this lesson formalizes

blocks.text: 1. What Independence Means

Two events are independent when the occurrence of one has absolutely no effect on the probability of the other. Formally, events A and B are independent if and only if P(A given B) equals P(A), equivalently P(B given A) equals P(B), using the conditional probability P(A given B) defined in the conditional probability lesson as the probability of A once you already know B has happened.

This is a strong, precise condition, not a vague sense that two things seem unrelated. If knowing B occurred shifts your estimate of A even slightly, the two events are dependent, no matter how small that shift is. Independence requires the shift to be exactly zero.

Independence is a property of the underlying random process being modeled, not something you can assume for convenience. Two fair, physically separate coin flips are independent because nothing links the mechanisms producing them. Two cards drawn from the same deck without replacement are not, because the first draw changes what remains for the second.

Because independence is a claim about the data generating process, it should be justified by reasoning about how the events arise, by direct empirical testing, or ideally both, rather than inferred purely from a single observed correlation number looking small.
2. Testing Independence: P(A given B) equals P(A)

The formal test for independence follows directly from the definition of conditional probability: compute P(A given B) and compare it to the plain, unconditional P(A). If the two match exactly, A and B are independent. If they differ at all, they are dependent, and the size and direction of that difference describes how much information B carries about A.

blocks.title: A concrete example
blocks.content: Let A be the event it rains tomorrow, and let B be the event a fair coin lands heads today. These two events are independent, since the coin has no causal or statistical connection to tomorrow's weather. P(rain given heads) equals P(rain) exactly, because knowing the coin outcome gives zero new information about the forecast.

blocks.text: Because the test is symmetric, checking P(B given A) equals P(B) gives exactly the same verdict as checking P(A given B) equals P(A). Either direction works, so in practice you use whichever conditional probability is easier to compute or already known from the data you have.
3. The Multiplication Rule as a Special Case

The general multiplication rule from probability rules states P(A and B) equals P(A given B) times P(B), true for any two events regardless of whether they are related. Independence simplifies this directly: substituting P(A given B) equals P(A) into the general rule collapses it down to P(A and B) equals P(A) times P(B), the simple product rule that was previewed in probability rules but only formally justified here.

code.content:
p_a = 0.5      # fair coin, first flip is heads
p_b = 0.5      # fair coin, second flip is heads
p_a_and_b = p_a * p_b
print(p_a_and_b)   # 0.25, valid only because the two flips are independent

blocks.text: This substitution is exactly why the simple multiplication P(A) times P(B) only ever applies to independent events. Applying it to dependent events silently produces a wrong answer, since it implicitly assumes a conditional probability equals its unconditional counterpart when that assumption does not actually hold.
Whenever you see P(A and B) computed as a plain product of two individual probabilities, treat it as an implicit claim of independence, one that deserves to be checked rather than taken on faith.
4. Independence Is Not Mutual Exclusivity

One of the most common mix-ups in probability is treating independent and mutually exclusive as synonyms, or even as compatible ideas. They are close to opposites. Mutually exclusive events cannot both happen, so P(A and B) equals 0. Independent events, by contrast, can typically both happen, and knowing one occurred tells you nothing about the other.

blocks.title: A concrete example
blocks.content: Roll a fair six sided die. Let A be the event the roll is 2, and let B be the event the roll is 5. These events are mutually exclusive, a single roll cannot be both 2 and 5. Are they independent? P(A) equals one sixth, but P(A given B) equals 0, since already knowing the roll is 5 rules out 2 entirely. Because 0 does not equal one sixth, A and B are dependent, not independent.

blocks.text: In fact, any two mutually exclusive events with nonzero individual probabilities are always dependent, never independent. If A and B cannot both occur, learning B happened tells you with certainty that A did not, so P(A given B) equals 0, which will not equal P(A) unless P(A) was already 0. Mutual exclusivity is itself a strong form of dependence, the strongest form of negative dependence there is.

items: Mutually exclusive means the events cannot occur together, P(A and B) equals 0.
Independent means occurrence of one carries no information about the other, P(A given B) equals P(A).
A pair of events can be neither mutually exclusive nor independent, for example two correlated but not contradictory outcomes.
A pair of events is essentially never both mutually exclusive and independent at once, unless one of them already has probability 0.

blocks.text: 5. Checking Independence Empirically

In real datasets, you rarely get to assume independence just because two variables look unrelated. A common practical check is to compare the observed joint frequency of A and B against the product of their marginal frequencies across a large enough sample. If the observed P(A and B) sits close to P(A) times P(B), independence is a reasonable working assumption. If it consistently drifts away, the events are dependent and should be modeled that way.

items: The joint frequency of A and B consistently differs from the product of their individual frequencies, even after collecting more data.
A domain reason exists for A and B to share a cause, for example both depend on the same underlying user, time period, or upstream feature.
A statistical test built for exactly this purpose, such as a chi square test of independence on a contingency table, rejects the independence hypothesis at a reasonable significance level.

blocks.text: None of these checks prove independence outright, since a limited sample can look independent purely by chance. They provide evidence for or against the assumption, which is normally the best that is practically available, and that evidence should be revisited whenever more data arrives.
6. Independence in Code

A quick way to sanity check an independence assumption in code is to simulate the process many times and compare the empirical joint probability against the product of the empirical marginal probabilities.

code.content:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 200000
flip1 = rng.integers(0, 2, n)
flip2 = rng.integers(0, 2, n)

p_a = np.mean(flip1 == 1)
p_b = np.mean(flip2 == 1)
p_both = np.mean((flip1 == 1) & (flip2 == 1))

print(p_a, p_b, p_both, p_a * p_b)
# p_both lands very close to p_a times p_b, exactly what independence predicts

blocks.text: With a large enough sample, the gap between the observed joint probability and the product of the marginals shrinks toward zero for genuinely independent processes, purely due to the law of large numbers. A gap that stays large and stable as the sample grows is a real signal of dependence, not sampling noise.
7. Visualizing Independent Events

A probability tree makes independence visually obvious. Draw two fair coin flips as a tree: the first flip branches into heads and tails, each with probability 0.5, and then each of those branches splits again into heads and tails, again each with probability 0.5. The key feature of independence is that the second level probabilities are identical no matter which branch you took at the first level.

blocks.alt: Probability tree for two independent coin flips
blocks.caption: The second flip stays at 0.5 regardless of the first outcome

blocks.text: Contrast this with a dependent process, such as drawing two cards from a deck without replacement. In that tree, the branch probabilities at the second level would differ depending on which card was drawn first, since removing a card changes what remains. Whenever a tree's later branch probabilities depend on the path taken to reach them, the underlying events are dependent.
8. Sampling With and Without Replacement

Drawing cards from a standard 52 card deck, which contains 4 aces, is a classic way to see independence appear and disappear based purely on how the sampling is done. P(first card is an ace) equals 4/52. If the first card is set aside and not returned to the deck, P(second card is an ace given first card was an ace) equals 3/51, which is different from the unconditional 4/52, so the two draws are dependent.

If instead the first card is returned to the deck and the deck is reshuffled before the second draw, P(second card is an ace) goes back to exactly 4/52 regardless of what the first card was, and the two draws become independent again. This is exactly why sampling with replacement is the standard trick used to make repeated draws independent.

code.content:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
trials = 200000

aces_no_replace = 0
aces_with_replace = 0
for _ in range(trials):
    deck = np.arange(52)
    rng.shuffle(deck)
    first, second = deck[0], deck[1]
    if first < 4 and second < 4:
        aces_no_replace += 1
    first_r = rng.integers(0, 52)
    second_r = rng.integers(0, 52)
    if first_r < 4 and second_r < 4:
        aces_with_replace += 1

print(aces_no_replace / trials)     # close to 1/221, about 0.0045
print(aces_with_replace / trials)   # close to 1/169, about 0.0059

blocks.text: 9. Independence Among More Than Two Events

Independence extends beyond a single pair of events to any number of events, but the extension needs a little care. With three or more events, checking every pair in isolation is not automatically enough to guarantee the strongest, most useful form of independence.
9.1 Pairwise Independence vs Mutual Independence

Events are pairwise independent if every pair among them satisfies the independence test on its own. Events are mutually independent, a stronger condition, if every subset of them, not just every pair, has a joint probability equal to the product of the individual probabilities in that subset. Mutual independence implies pairwise independence, but the reverse is not true.

blocks.title: A concrete example
blocks.content: Flip a fair coin twice. Let A be the event the first flip is heads, B be the event the second flip is heads, and C be the event the two flips agree, both heads or both tails. Each pair among A, B, and C is independent on its own. But knowing both A and B tells you C with certainty, so all three together are not mutually independent, even though every pair passes the independence test.

blocks.text: Most theorems used in statistics and machine learning, including the law of large numbers and the central limit theorem in their standard forms, require the stronger mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence, so it is worth checking which one an assumption actually needs.
10. The i.i.d. Assumption in Machine Learning

Most machine learning theory assumes training examples are independent and identically distributed, commonly abbreviated i.i.d.: each example is drawn independently of every other example, and all examples come from the same underlying distribution. This assumption underlies most generalization bounds, and it is exactly why a held out test set is treated as behaving like a fresh, independent draw from the same distribution as the training data.

When the i.i.d. assumption is violated, evaluation can become badly overconfident. Time series data with strong autocorrelation, where each example is influenced by the ones just before it, breaks independence. Duplicate or near duplicate records that leak between the training set and the test set break independence too, since the model effectively gets to see part of the test answer during training.

items: Shuffling a dataset before splitting into train and test helps satisfy the identically distributed part of the assumption, but does nothing to fix genuine dependence between examples, such as duplicated rows.

Grouped data, such as multiple records from the same user or the same time window, should usually be split by group rather than by row, otherwise training and test examples from the same group are not truly independent draws.
A model that performs unexpectedly well on a held out set is worth double checking for exactly this kind of independence violation before celebrating the result.

blocks.text: 11. Naive Bayes and the Independence Assumption

The naive Bayes classifier gets its name directly from an independence assumption: conditioned on the class label, every feature is assumed independent of every other feature. That turns the otherwise intractable joint likelihood P(features given class) into a simple product, P(feature one given class) times P(feature two given class) times every other feature's conditional probability, each of which is easy to estimate on its own.

code.content:
p_spam = 0.4
p_ham = 0.6

# naive bayes assumes features are conditionally independent given the class,
# so the joint likelihood is just a product of per feature likelihoods
p_free_given_spam, p_win_given_spam = 0.7, 0.6
p_free_given_ham, p_win_given_ham = 0.05, 0.02

score_spam = p_spam * p_free_given_spam * p_win_given_spam
score_ham = p_ham * p_free_given_ham * p_win_given_ham
print(score_spam, score_ham)   # spam wins by a wide margin, even though "free"
                                # and "win" are correlated in real emails, not
                                # truly independent given the spam label

blocks.text: The word naive is a deliberate admission that this conditional independence assumption is almost never literally true. Words like free and win tend to show up together in spam far more often than independence would predict. Yet naive Bayes classifiers still perform surprisingly well in practice, because classification only requires the correct class to come out on top of the ranking, not a perfectly calibrated probability.
12. Independence Assumptions Elsewhere in AI

Independence assumptions show up throughout machine learning well beyond naive Bayes. Dropout during neural network training treats each unit's random deactivation as an independent event. Mini batch stochastic gradient descent assumes each batch is drawn independently from the overall training distribution, which is part of why shuffling the data before each training epoch matters. Monte Carlo estimation, used for everything from Bayesian posterior approximation to reinforcement learning rollouts, leans on independent samples so the law of large numbers guarantees the estimate converges to the true value.

In practice, independence is almost always a simplification of a messier reality, and its silent violation is one of the most common sources of subtle bugs, quietly biased models, or overconfident uncertainty estimates. Treating an assumption of independence as a hypothesis to be checked, rather than a fact to be trusted, is one of the most valuable habits a practitioner can build.
13. Common Notation for Independence

A small amount of shorthand notation recurs across textbooks and papers whenever independence is discussed. Recognizing it quickly makes reading probability heavy material, including most machine learning papers, considerably faster.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Notation","Meaning"],"rows":[["A and B independent","P(A and B) equals P(A) times P(B)"],["P(A given B) equals P(A)","occurrence of B gives no information about A"],["A1, A2, and so on mutually independent","every subset of the events multiplies as expected, not just each pair"],["i.i.d.","independent and identically distributed, the standard assumption for training data in machine learning"]]}

blocks.text: Some texts write A independent of B using a special perpendicular symbol instead of spelling the word out, but the underlying meaning is always the same equality between a conditional probability and its unconditional counterpart covered throughout this lesson.
14. A Worked Example

Suppose you track 100 days of weather and commuting data. On 30 of those days it rained, and on 40 of those days your bus was late, with both rain and a late bus happening together on 12 days. If rain and a late bus were independent, you would expect the joint frequency to equal P(rain) times P(late bus), which is 0.30 times 0.40, or 0.12, meaning 12 out of 100 days. The observed 12 days matches that prediction almost exactly, so in this sample, rain and a late bus behave as independent.

Now suppose over the same 100 days, your alarm failed to go off on 10 days, and you were late for work on 15 days, with both happening together on 8 days. If alarm failure and being late for work were independent, you would expect 0.10 times 0.15, or 0.015, meaning roughly 1.5 out of 100 days. The observed 8 days is more than five times higher than that prediction, a clear sign that alarm failure and being late are strongly dependent, which matches the obvious causal story.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Event pair","P(A)","P(B)","P(A) times P(B)","Observed P(A and B)","Independent?"],"rows":[["Rain, bus late","0.30","0.40","0.12","0.12","Yes, closely matches"],["Alarm fails, late for work","0.10","0.15","0.015","0.08","No, much higher than expected"]]}

blocks.text: This is exactly the pattern to look for whenever you are handed a real dataset and asked whether two variables can be treated as independent: compute the expected joint probability under independence, compare it to what actually happened, and let the size of the gap tell you whether the assumption is reasonable.
15. Common Mistakes

items: Assuming two events are independent simply because they seem unrelated on the surface, without checking or testing the assumption against real data.
Confusing independence with mutual exclusivity, when mutually exclusive events with nonzero probability are actually dependent, as covered earlier in this lesson.
Applying the simple product rule P(A and B) equals P(A) times P(B) to events that are actually dependent, silently producing a wrong joint probability.

Committing the gambler's fallacy, believing a fair coin is due for tails after a run of heads, when each flip remains independent of every prior flip and the true probability of tails stays exactly 0.5 regardless of history.
Treating a small sample that happens to look independent as proof of independence, rather than as weak, inconclusive evidence that could easily be a coincidence.

blocks.text: Almost every one of these mistakes has the same root cause: treating independence as a default assumption rather than a specific, testable claim about how the data was generated.
16. Practice: Test Independence in Code

The exercise below simulates two independent dice rolls and confirms that conditioning on the first roll does not change the probability of the second. Run it, confirm the two printed numbers land close together, then extend it to the dependent case described in the comment.

code.content:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
n = 500000

# Independent draws: two separate fair dice
die1 = rng.integers(1, 7, n)
die2 = rng.integers(1, 7, n)
p_die2_is_6 = np.mean(die2 == 6)
p_die2_is_6_given_die1_is_6 = np.mean(die2[die1 == 6] == 6)
print(p_die2_is_6, p_die2_is_6_given_die1_is_6)   # should be nearly identical

# TODO: extend this simulation to drawing two cards without replacement from a
# 52 card deck (4 aces). Compute P(second card is an ace) and compare it to
# P(second card is an ace given first card was an ace). They should differ,
# confirming the two draws are dependent, unlike the two dice above.

blocks.text: If your extension is correct, the two dice probabilities should agree to within simulation noise, while the two card probabilities should show a clear, repeatable gap, exactly matching the with replacement versus without replacement comparison worked through earlier in this lesson.
Key Takeaway

Independence is the precise condition P(A given B) equals P(A), knowing one event occurred gives you zero information about the other, and it is the special case that collapses the general multiplication rule P(A and B) equals P(A given B) times P(B) down to the simple product P(A) times P(B). It is easy to confuse with mutual exclusivity, but mutually exclusive events with nonzero probability are actually dependent, since ruling one in rules the other out completely.

Independence is also one of the quiet workhorses of applied machine learning, underlying the i.i.d. assumption behind most generalization theory and the conditional independence assumption that gives naive Bayes both its simplicity and its name. Treat every independence claim as a hypothesis worth testing against real data rather than a convenient default, and you will avoid the most common and most costly mistakes covered in this lesson.
